text: Now look beyond them. Beyond the last roofs, beyond the walls, to the west. There is another light out there. Not amber. Not warm. A duller glow, and a low haze, and the smell of smoke that does not come from any kitchen. That is the camp. That is where the army is. And that is where our story will go, in a little while. But not yet. For now, stay here, at this window. Let the city be a city for a few more minutes. Let the lamps be lamps, and the bell be a bell, and the dog in the street be a dog, sleeping in the exact centre of the road, in the way of everyone, and caring nothing for any of it. Because the truth is this: on the last night of a city, the most important things are never the walls. They are the small things that everyone does without thinking, and that nobody will do again. When you are ready, we will walk down from this tower, and we will go to the wall.

The wall of Constantinople is not one wall. It is a system. If you have heard of it, you have probably heard the number: the Theodosian Walls, built in the fifth century, eleven hundred years before this night, and still, in 1453, the strongest fortification in the world. But numbers do not tell you what it feels like to stand beside it. So let us stand beside it. The first thing you notice is that the wall is not flat. It has a rhythm. It steps. Every few dozen paces, a tower pushes out from the line, and the line steps forward, and the tower gives the defenders a place to stand and look along the face of the wall instead of straight out at the enemy. This is not decoration. This is a machine made of stone. Behind the tower, the wall goes on, and behind the wall, there is another wall. And behind that, another. And in front of everything, there is a ditch. A moat, wide and deep, cut into the ground so that anyone attacking has to climb down before they can climb up.

The defenders can stand on three levels. The attackers have to cross three thresholds. For a thousand years, this was enough. Tonight, the wall is quiet. The men on it are not standing in ranks. They are sitting. Some are leaning against the battlements with their helmets off, and their hair flat with sweat, and their eyes half closed. Some are mending. Some are eating bread and hard cheese, in the slow way of men who have learned that eating is a thing worth doing properly, even now. There are not many of them. This is the thing that no painting ever shows you. The wall is enormous. The garrison is tiny. Nine thousand people in a city built for half a million. They are spread so thinly along the line that in some places, a single man is responsible for a stretch of wall longer than a street. And they have been doing this for weeks.

So they have developed a kind of rhythm. A watch, and a sleep, and a meal, and a watch again. They have learned where the wind comes through, and where a man can lie down without being seen by an officer, and which section of the parapet is warmest in the early morning. They have made a home of the wall. Let us walk along it for a while, from tower to tower, and listen. The first tower is quiet. Two men, both asleep. One of them is snoring, very softly, in that uneven way that is somehow more restful to hear than to do. The second tower is quiet too, but there is a lamp in it, and by the lamp, a young man is writing. He has a small piece of paper, and a stub of charcoal, and he is writing very slowly. If we look over his shoulder, and we will not, because it is not kind, we would see that it is not a letter. It is a list. A list of small things. The name of a street. The name of a bakery. The colour of a door.

Men do this, on the last night of a world. They write down small things, because the large things are too large to write. The third tower has a lamp, and a jug of water, and three men who are not asleep. They are talking in low voices. Not about the army outside, but about a river. One of them is from a village on a river, and he is describing it: the way the water goes over the stones in spring, and the way you can catch a certain kind of small fish with your hands if you stand very still. The other two are listening. Nobody is saying: this is the last conversation we will have. Nobody is saying anything like that. They are just listening to a man describe a river, and in the listening, there is a kind of gentleness that is hard to put into words. This is what people do, when the end is near. They do not speak of the end. They speak of rivers.

Now look out. Over the parapet, into the dark. You cannot see much. The moon is thin tonight, and the mist has come up from the water, and the ground in front of the wall has gone the colour of old iron. But if you are patient, if you stand there, and let your eyes get used to the dark, you will begin to see shapes. Tents. Hundreds of them. Then more, further off, and more beyond those, until the ground is no longer ground but a city of canvas, laid out in lines and rows the way a proper camp is laid out, because whoever commands it has done this before. And in the middle of that camp, there is a shape that does not look like a tent. It is longer than a house. It is darker than the dark. It sits on wheels as tall as a man. You will see it properly later. For now, let us simply notice it, and feel what the men on the wall feel when they look at it. They do not talk about it. They have stopped talking about it.

The last tower on our walk has a lamp with a little door in it, and the lamp is turned low. There is a man sitting on the step, with his back against the stone, and his eyes closed. He is not asleep. You can tell by his hands. They are not loose. They are folded, and still, in the way of a man who is thinking. He is thinking about tomorrow. Not in the way we would think about it. Not with fear, or with plans. He is thinking about it the way you think about a long journey: the shape of it, the beginning, and the part in the middle, and the arriving. He has already packed. In his mind, he has already packed. And now there is nothing to do but wait. Let us leave him there. He has earned the quiet. Let us go back down into the city, and warm our hands, and take a cup of something hot, and let the wall be a wall for a little while. Because in the morning, the wall will be something else.

Now let us cross the ditch. This is not an easy thing to ask of you. But we are only walking. Nobody will stop us. On this night, the ground between the two sides is the quietest place in the world. It is a strip of bare earth, and broken stone, and thin grass, and it belongs to no one. Halfway across, stop, and turn around, and look back at the city. It is beautiful. That is the strange and terrible thing. From here, with the mist around your feet and the hills beyond, the city looks like something in a book. The lamps along the top of the wall. The domes in the distance. The bell, for a moment, still ringing. You would not know, from here, that anything was wrong. Now turn back, and walk on into the camp.

The first thing that reaches you is the smell. Woodsmoke, and horse, and wet canvas, and something cooking that you cannot name. The second thing is the sound. Not shouting. Not marching. The ordinary sound of a very large number of men doing very small things: talking, coughing, sharpening, laughing once, and then going quiet. The camp is laid out in lines. There are streets between the tents, and the streets are swept. There are latrines, dug in rows, away from the water. There is a place where the animals are kept, and a place where the food is cooked, and a place where a man can sit and have his hair cut, if he has something to trade for it. It is a city too. That is what nobody tells you about a siege. A siege is two cities, looking at each other.

Let us walk down the main street. Let us keep to the edge, where the shadows are, and let us not disturb anyone. Here is a tent with the flap pinned back. Inside, by a small lamp, a man is repairing a boot. He has a needle made of bone, and a length of waxed thread, and he is working slowly, pressing the needle through the leather with a small wooden clamp. His hands are careful. He is not thinking about the city. He is thinking about the boot. Here is another tent, and inside it, someone is singing, very quietly, in a language you do not know, a song with only four or five notes in it, going round and round. It is not a sad song. It is a song to work by, or to fall asleep to. It stops. There is a murmur. Then it starts again.
